title: Guiding Image Generators

thumbnail.headline: Brief It Like a Photographer
thumbnail.image: Navy background, three poster drafts in a row getting clearer and warmer from left to right, the last with empty sky at the top, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Brief It Like a Photographer
slide.body: Three poster thumbnails labelled v1, v2, v3: a plain loaf in the dark → warm baskets of bread → baskets in the lower half with clear sky on top. Small tag: Generative AI Explained · Lesson 6.

production_notes: Screen demo tool: Google Gemini image generation (Gemini app or Google AI Studio), as chosen in DECISIONS.md. Backup: Adobe Firefly free tier.

[VERSION] Before recording, confirm the demo steps against the live tool: how to choose a portrait aspect ratio (menu, button or in the prompt), how to generate, and how to show three results side by side. Also check free limits, whether number of images, style presets or negative prompts exist, and the licence terms for using generated images in advertising.
If the tool has no aspect-ratio control, add 'tall portrait format' to each prompt on screen and change the scene 9 voiceover to match.

The generated images will differ from those described in content.md. Pick runs that show the described problems (v1 dark and generic; v2 full to the edges) or adjust the voiceover to describe what actually appears.
The poster text (bakery name and opening hours) is added afterwards in a design tool; show it briefly but do not name a design tool brand in the voiceover.
Wanjiru and her Nairobi bakery are fictional; do not show a real bakery name or logo. Use a clean demo Google account.

Hook.voiceover: You type bread into an image generator and get a plain loaf on a white table. It is not wrong, but it is not what you imagined. The model filled every gap with the most typical choice. So how do you guide it?

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you saw that the prompt steers every step, and that the model fills in anything you do not describe. So a better prompt does not need magic words. It simply gives clearer guidance on the details that matter to you.

A useful checklist has six parts. The subject, meaning what is in the image. Say round loaves and small rolls, not just bread. The setting, meaning where it is. And the style, for example a realistic photograph, a flat illustration or a watercolour painting.

slide.title: Six-part checklist (1 to 3)
slide.body: 1. Subject: what is in it ('round loaves and small rolls') 2. Setting: where it is ('outdoor market stall') 3. Style: photo, flat illustration, watercolour

Explain.voiceover: Then the composition, meaning how the image is arranged. A close-up, a wide view, or empty space at the top for a title. The lighting, like soft morning sunlight or warm evening light. And the aspect ratio, the shape of the image. Many tools set this with a menu, not in the prompt.

slide.title: Six-part checklist (4 to 6)
slide.body: 4. Composition: close-up, wide view, space for a title 5. Lighting: soft morning sun, warm evening light 6. Aspect ratio: square, tall, wide (often a menu)

Explain.voiceover: Some generators also offer extra settings, such as the number of images, a style preset, or a list of things to avoid. These differ between tools, so look around the settings before you start.

slide.title: Extra settings (vary by tool)
slide.body: Number of images · Style preset · Things to avoid (negative prompt). Caption: check your tool's settings first

Explain.voiceover: Two more tips. Change one or two things at a time, so you can see which change caused which effect. And do not ask for exact text inside the image. Image models often get letters wrong. Add the text later in a design tool.

slide.title: Two more tips
slide.body: Change one or two things at a time · No exact text inside the image: add it later in a design tool

Explain.voiceover: Think of it like briefing a photographer you cannot speak to again. If you only say, take a photo of bread, they choose the place, the angle and the light themselves. A clear brief brings the result much closer to what you had in mind.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's try it. Wanjiru runs a small bakery in Nairobi. She wants a poster image of fresh bread on a market stall, to advertise her weekend stall. We will use the Gemini app, but any free image generator works.
Demonstrate.stock_query: fresh bread baskets at outdoor market

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, she opens the image generator and chooses a tall, portrait shape, because the poster is tall. Then she types her first version. Bread on a market stall.
screen_steps: Open Google Gemini image generation and start a new chat
Type version 1: 'bread on a market stall' and generate

Demonstrate.voiceover: The result shows a generic loaf on a grey table, in a dark setting. It does not look fresh, local or inviting. Four words left almost everything to the model. So she adds the subject, the setting and the lighting.
screen_steps: Show the version 1 image full size
Type version 2: 'Fresh round loaves and small brown bread rolls in woven baskets on a wooden market stall, soft morning sunlight.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: Version two looks fresh and warm. Much better. But the image is full to the edges, and there is no space for the poster title. So she adds style and composition. A realistic photograph, a close-up, baskets in the lower half, and plain light sky in the upper half for a title.
screen_steps: Show the version 2 image and point to the full edges

Type version 3: 'Realistic photograph of fresh round loaves and small brown bread rolls in woven baskets on a wooden market stall, soft morning sunlight, close-up, baskets in the lower half, plain light sky in the upper half for a title.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now she compares all three side by side. Each change fixed one problem. Version three has empty sky at the top, ready for the bakery name and opening hours, which she adds later in a design tool so the letters are correct.
screen_steps: Place the three images side by side with their prompts
Label what each change improved: v2 fresh and warm, v3 space for a title
Briefly show the poster with the bakery name and hours added in a design tool

Demonstrate.voiceover: Before printing, she checks the image closely for strange details. She also checks the tool's terms, to confirm she may use the image in advertising.
screen_steps: Zoom into the version 3 image to check the baskets and bread for strange details
Open the tool's terms page and scroll to the section on using generated images

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to add words like amazing, ultra-detailed and masterpiece, hoping for better quality. They rarely help, and very long prompts can confuse the model. Describe the six parts clearly, and use the tool's settings instead.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the model fills every gap with typical patterns, so a clear prompt gives better guidance. Second, describe subject, setting, style, composition and lighting, and choose the aspect ratio in the settings when you can. Third, improve in small steps, and add exact text in a design tool, not in the prompt.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Gaps get typical patterns: guide clearly. 2. Subject, setting, style, composition, lighting + aspect ratio. 3. Small steps; add text later.

CTA.voiceover: Your turn. In the exercise below, write three versions of an image prompt for a business of your choice, such as a tea stall or a language school. Then generate each one, and note what each change improved. It takes about twenty-five minutes. Next, we look at multimodal models, with text, images and audio together. See you there.
